title: Why React Exists
summary: See why hand-written DOM updates break down, how React grew out of the jQuery and MVC years, and why teams pick it over plain JavaScript.
intro: Every page that responds to people has the same job underneath: when the data changes, the screen has to change to match, everywhere that data shows. Done by hand, that job is where a lot of frontend bugs come from: a count that's off, a button that stopped responding, a box that lost what you were typing. React exists to take the job off your hands. This lesson starts with the problem in plain JavaScript, follows the tools that tried to solve it before React, then explains the idea React is built on, what React is made of, and when it's worth what it costs.

steps.title: Hand-written DOM updates break down
steps.body:
React's rules can look fussy at first: give each list item a key, never change state directly, keep components free of side effects. Each rule is there to prevent a bug you'd otherwise write by hand. This part shows those bugs, in the plain JavaScript you know from the web course.

## The data and its views

Recall how the web course kept a page in sync: the data lives in variables, and the DOM is a **view** of it, one way of showing it. Take a small shop. Its data is the cart, and four places on the page show it:

- a badge in the header: Cart: 2
- the total on the cart panel: $223.00
- the Add button on each product, which turns into Added
- a banner that says how much more to spend for free shipping

Adding a product means updating every one of them:

```javascript sketch
function addToCart(product) {
  cart.push(product);
  document.querySelector("#cart-count").textContent = `Cart: ${cart.length}`;
  document.querySelector("#cart-total").textContent = formatPrice(totalCents(cart));
  document.querySelector(`[data-slug="${product.slug}"] .add`).textContent = "Added";
  // ...and the free shipping banner?
}
```

## One change, many places

That's one function. The cart also changes when someone removes a product, changes a quantity, checks out, or comes back and the cart loads from the server. Each of those five functions has to update all four places. That's twenty pieces of update code, and when a designer adds a fifth place, like a cart total in the page title, you have to find all five functions and add it to each.

```diagram why-react-fan-out
One change to the data has to reach four places by hand, and one was forgotten.
```

## Three ways it goes wrong

**Forgotten updates.** In the diagram, nobody wrote the banner's update. The order already ships free, and the banner still asks for $16.00 more. There's no error and nothing in the console: just a page that disagrees with itself, which someone notices weeks later.

**Lost focus and typing.** The tempting fix is one `render` function that rebuilds the whole page from the data with `innerHTML`, called after every change. Now nothing can be forgotten, since every place is rebuilt each time. But every rebuild throws away the old elements and makes new ones. The box someone was typing in is replaced by a new box, and the new one doesn't have the **focus**, the browser's marker for which element gets the keys you press. A list someone scrolled jumps back to the top. An animation starts over. And a long list gets slow, since the browser rebuilds all of it for every key press. The example below shows the focus problem.

**Stale listeners.** Rebuilt elements lose the event listeners attached to the old ones, so a button can quietly stop responding. Run the setup code twice to fix that, and a button can end up with two listeners, so one click adds two packs. Event delegation, one listener on a parent that checks what was clicked, avoids this, but every handler now works out what was clicked from `data-` attributes.

## The real question

None of these bugs comes from a careless line. They come from the approach: you're writing the steps that change the page, by hand, for every change. So the real question is how the page can follow the data by itself, without throwing away what the person is doing. The rest of this lesson is about how people answered that, and React's answer.

examples.title: A render function that rebuilds everything
examples.prompt: A small search page in plain JavaScript, `app.js`, loaded by a page with an empty `<div id="app">`. Click in the search box and type te.
examples.explanation: The data is the `state` object, and `render` draws the whole page from it, so the cart count and the list can never disagree. Both listeners sit on `#app`, which is never replaced, so they survive every rebuild. That's event delegation at work. But look at what typing does. The first letter, t, fires the input event, the handler saves it in `state.query`, and `render` replaces everything inside `#app`, the search box included. The new box shows t, since `render` wrote it into the `value`, but nothing has focus anymore: `document.activeElement`, the element with the focus, is the page's `<body>`, which is what the console printed. So the e you typed next went nowhere, and the box still says t. There's a second problem too: the query goes into HTML unescaped, so typing a `"` breaks the page, the injection risk the web course warned about with `innerHTML`.

steps.title: From jQuery to React
steps.body:
React didn't appear out of nowhere. It was one answer, among several, to the problem in the previous part, and each answer before it left a mark you'll still see at work: old jQuery sites, AngularJS apps being moved to something newer, React code written before 2019. Knowing the order helps you read all of it.

```diagram why-react-timeline
Each tool kept what worked before it and changed the part that didn't.
```

## jQuery, 2006: shorter steps

Recall jQuery from the web course. In 2006, every browser did the DOM a little differently, and jQuery gave you one short way to find elements, change them, and listen for events that worked in all of them. It made each step easier to write. It didn't change the approach, though: you still wrote the steps, and a big jQuery app became a tangle of handlers that changed the page in ways other handlers didn't expect.

## Backbone and AngularJS, 2010: models and views

The next tools borrowed **MVC**, model-view-controller, an older way to organize programs with a screen. The **model** holds the data, the **view** shows it, and the **controller** is the code that connects the two. Split that way, the data gets one home, instead of living partly in variables and partly in the page.

**Backbone.js** gave you models that announce every change and views that listen for those announcements and draw themselves again. That organized the code, but you still wired each view to each model by hand, and a view drew itself again with `innerHTML`, so the focus problem came along.

**AngularJS**, from Google, went further with **two-way data binding**: you wrote `{{ query }}` in the HTML, and AngularJS kept the page and the variable in step in both directions. Change the variable and the page changes. Type in a bound box and the variable changes. It did this with the **digest cycle**: after every event, AngularJS checked every value the page used to see whether it had changed, then updated the page, then checked again in case that update changed something else. In a small app it felt like magic. In a big one, thousands of checks ran on every key press, and with data flowing both ways, it got hard to tell what had changed what. Google stopped supporting AngularJS at the end of 2021. **Angular**, a separate framework from the same team, replaced it.

## React, 2013: draw it again, change the difference

React started at Facebook, made by an engineer named Jordan Walke, and ran Facebook's news feed and then Instagram before it was released for everyone in 2013. Its idea sounded wasteful: whenever the data changes, describe the whole UI again from scratch, the way a `render` function does. The trick is that the description isn't the DOM. It's a light copy of the page made of plain JavaScript objects, which people came to call the **virtual DOM**. React compares the new copy with the last one and changes only the real DOM that differs. You get the simplicity of rebuilding everything, without the lost focus or the slowness, and data flows one way only, from the data to the page.

The description was written in **JSX**, HTML-like tags right inside JavaScript. Many developers disliked it at first, since they'd been taught to keep HTML and JavaScript apart. It won them over because a piece of UI and the code that drives it change together, so keeping them in one file made sense.

## React since then

- **2015:** React Native brought the same React to phone apps.
- **2019:** **Hooks**, like `useState`, let a plain function component hold state. Before that, a component that held state had to be a JavaScript class. You'll still see class components in older code, as in the second example below.
- **2022:** React 18 added **concurrent rendering**: React can pause work on a big, slow update to handle a click first, then carry on.
- **2024:** React 19 made **Actions**, React's way of handling forms that send data, and **Server Components**, components that run only on the server, part of stable React.
- **2025:** the **React Compiler** 1.0, a build step that makes components skip work they don't need to redo, a job developers used to do by hand.

examples.title: Two-way binding in AngularJS
examples.prompt: A search box and a line of text bound to the same variable, as AngularJS code from around 2012 wrote them.
examples.code: Searching for: {{ query }}
examples.explanation: `ng-app` marks the part of the page AngularJS manages, and `ng-init` sets a variable, `query`, to empty text. `ng-model="query"` binds the box to that variable, and `{{ query }}` shows it. Type in the box and the variable changes, then the digest cycle notices and changes the paragraph. Change `query` in code and the box changes too. There's no listener and no DOM code at all, which is why it felt like magic. The cost was hidden: every `{{ }}` and every `ng-model` added a value to check after every event. React kept the part where you describe the page instead of changing it, and dropped the two-way flow.

examples.title: A component before hooks
examples.prompt: A counting button written as a class component, the way React code held state before 2019.
examples.explanation: This does what a hooks version with `useState` does: a button that counts. Here the component is a class that extends React's `Component`. Its data lives in `this.state`, it changes with `this.setState`, and its `render` method returns the JSX. React still calls `render` again after every change and updates only what differs, so the idea is the same. Classes made sharing logic between components awkward, and `this` caused its own bugs, which is why hooks replaced them. You'll write function components with hooks in this course, but it helps to recognize this shape in older code, since React still runs it.

steps.title: UI as a function of state
steps.body:
This part is the idea every React feature is built on. Once it clicks, the rules in later lessons stop looking arbitrary, because each one follows from it. ## Imperative and declarative There are two ways to tell a computer what you want. **Imperative** code gives the steps: find the badge, set its text, find the banner, set its text. **Declarative** code describes the result: the badge shows how many items are in the cart. It's the difference between giving a taxi driver every turn and giving them the address. The web course's DOM code is imperative: ```javascript sketch badge.textContent = `Cart: ${cart.length}`; banner.hidden = totalCents(cart) >= 5000; ``` React code is declarative. You write what the badge is, for any cart, and React does the steps: ```tsx sketch Cart: {cart.length} {totalCents(cart) < 5000 &&

Spend a little more for free shipping.

} ``` The declarative version holds for every value of `cart`. There's no "after adding" or "after removing" version to forget. ## State **State** is the data that can change while the page is open and that the screen depends on: the cart, the text in the search box, whether a menu is open. React's central idea is that the UI is a function of state. Give it the same state and you get the same screen, every time. To change the screen, you change the state, and never the page directly. ## Components A **component** is one of those functions, for one piece of the UI. It takes data and returns what that piece should look like. Components nest like HTML elements: an `App` holds a `Header`, which holds a `CartBadge`, and a `ProductList` holds one `ProductCard` for each product. Each can be read, reused, and tested on its own. ## Data down, events up A parent component passes data to its children as **props**, short for properties, written like attributes on an HTML tag: ``. A child never changes its props. When something happens inside a child, like a click, the child calls a function its parent gave it, and the parent changes the state. The new state flows down to the children again. This is **one-way data flow**: data goes down, and events go up. It's the opposite of AngularJS's two-way binding, and it's what makes bugs findable. For any value on screen, there's one place it comes from and one place it can change, so when the badge is wrong, you know where to look. ## Elements, trees, and diffing What does a component actually return? Not DOM elements. It returns **React elements**: small, plain JavaScript objects that describe what should be on screen, like an object saying this is an `h2` with the text Trail Pack 45L. Together they form an **element tree**, shaped like the DOM you want. ```diagram why-react-ui-from-state React compares the new tree with the last one, and makes only the DOM changes that the difference needs. ``` Follow the diagram. In step 1, the state changes: the cart count goes from 2 to 3. In step 2, React calls the component again, and in step 3 it returns a new element tree. Making objects is cheap, much cheaper than changing the DOM. In step 4, React compares the new tree with the last one, node by node. That comparison is called **diffing**, and React's name for the whole process is **reconciliation**. It finds one difference: the span's text. In step 5, React makes that one DOM change. The heading and everything else keep their DOM elements, so the focus, anything typed, and the scroll position all survive. The Re-rendering and Performance lesson goes deep into how the comparison works.

examples.title: The cart summary, declared
examples.prompt: The shop's cart panel as a component, `src/components/CartSummary.tsx`. It gets the cart's items from its parent, and works out everything it shows from them.
examples.output:
Cart: 2

Total: $223.00

Your order ships free.
examples.explanation: This is the panel from the first part, done declaratively. The `type` line is TypeScript, describing one item in the cart, and `items: CartItem[]` says the component gets a list of them. Every time React calls `CartSummary`, it works out the count, the total, and what's left for free shipping from `items`, with `reduce` adding them up. Then the JSX says what to show, with the `? :` choosing which line the banner gets. Nothing here adds to a cart or changes a page. The output is the panel's text, as the browser showed it, for a cart holding a kettle and a pack. A cart with only the $34.00 kettle would show Spend $16.00 more for free shipping. There's no way for the banner to fall behind, because there's no code that updates it: it's worked out from the same data as everything else, every time.

steps.title: React, React DOM, and frameworks
steps.body:
When you install React, you get two packages, and neither one shows pages at different URLs or fetches data. Knowing what's in the box, and what isn't, tells you which tool to reach for when you need the rest.

## Two packages

**`react`** holds what every React app needs, wherever it runs: components, elements, and **hooks**, the functions like `useState` that give components their abilities. It knows nothing about browsers.

**`react-dom`** connects React to a browser page. It's the part that makes, changes, and removes real DOM elements to match the element tree. It comes in pieces you import separately:

- `react-dom/client` starts React in a page. Its `createRoot` takes one DOM element and hands everything inside it to React.
- `react-dom/server` turns components into HTML on a server, which the Rendering React on the Server lesson uses.

Why two packages? The work of calling components and comparing trees is the same wherever the UI ends up. Only the last step, making real things on a real screen, changes. **React Native** is a third package that does that last step for phone apps: the same components, turned into a phone's own buttons and text instead of HTML. So `react` is the same in both, and the package under it decides where things appear.

## A build step

Browsers don't understand JSX, since it isn't JavaScript. React code is also usually written in **TypeScript**, JavaScript with **types** added: notes like `name: string` that say what kind of value each thing holds, so your editor can point out a mistake, like a misspelled property, before the page ever runs. Browsers don't understand types either.

So a React project needs a build step: a tool that turns `.tsx` files into plain JavaScript. It rewrites the JSX into ordinary function calls and removes the types. You met the tool that does this in the web course: Vite, which does it on the fly while you work and all at once when you build for production. That's why a React project always starts from a tool, which Starting a New React Project covers.

## What React leaves out

React draws the UI from state, and that's all it does, on purpose. It leaves these to other tools:

- **Routing:** showing a different screen for each URL, with Back and Forward working, which the web course did by hand with the History API.
- **Server data:** fetching it, keeping copies so the next screen is instant, and refreshing them when they go out of date.
- **The server:** making HTML before the browser gets it, and deciding which code runs where.

React helps with some of this, like Actions for forms that send data and `react-dom/server` for HTML, but it has no full answer to any of them. That's what makes it a library rather than a framework: it does one job and fits in with whatever you choose for the rest.

## Where the other tools fit

| You need | Tool | Where in the course |
|---|---|---|
| Components and state | `react` | React Basics |
| Showing them in a browser | `react-dom` | Starting a New React Project |
| A URL for each screen | React Router | Routing and App Structure |
| Server data and caching | TanStack Query | Calling APIs From React |
| HTML made on a server | `react-dom/server`, or Next.js | Rendering React on the Server, and the Next.js course |

**Next.js** is a framework that bundles all of these together: routing, data, server rendering, and the build. Recall from the web course that a framework built on top of a UI library like React is called a meta-framework. React's own documentation suggests starting a new production app with one. This course starts without one, so you see each piece and what it does. The Next.js course then shows what a framework adds.

examples.title: Where the two packages meet
examples.prompt: The file that starts every new Vite React app, `src/main.tsx`, as Vite writes it. It imports from both packages.
examples.code:
import { StrictMode } from 'react'
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'
import './index.css'
import App from './App.tsx'

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <App />
  </StrictMode>,
)
examples.explanation: `StrictMode` comes from `react`: it's a component that adds extra checks while you develop. `createRoot` comes from `react-dom/client`. `document.getElementById('root')` finds an empty `<div id="root">` in the page's HTML, and `createRoot` hands it to React. The `!` after it is TypeScript, promising the element exists. `.render(...)` then gives React the element tree to draw there: your whole app, `App`, wrapped in `StrictMode`. After this one call, React owns everything inside that div, and you never touch it directly. Vite writes this file without semicolons and with single quotes, a style some teams prefer. The course's own code uses double quotes and semicolons, and both work the same. Starting a New React Project explains every line, and how the page boots.

steps.title: Why React over plain JavaScript
steps.body:
React isn't free, and a good web developer can say when it's worth what it costs. This part weighs both sides, so you can make that call on your own projects.

## What you get

- **Reusable components.** One `ProductCard` serves the product list, the search results, and the related products under each product page. Fix a bug in it once, and it's fixed everywhere.
- **Testable pieces.** A component is a function: give it props, and check what it shows. The Testing lessons do exactly that.
- **Bugs you can trace.** With data flowing one way, every value on screen has one source. When something's wrong, you follow it up the tree.
- **The ecosystem.** Libraries exist for almost everything an app needs: routing, server data, forms, charts, and menus and dialogs that already work with keyboards and screen readers. Most are written for React first.
- **Tools.** React DevTools shows the component tree, each component's props and state, and why a component ran again.
- **People.** So many developers know React that a team can hire for it, and you can read a new team's code on your first day.

## What it costs

**JavaScript to download and run.** A React app can't respond until the browser has downloaded React, read it, and run it. The example below builds the starter app Vite makes, before you've written a line of your own: its JavaScript is 222 kB, or 69 kB once compressed for the trip, and most of that is React and React DOM. On a fast laptop that's nothing. On a cheap phone on a slow network, it's time spent looking at a page that doesn't respond yet, which the web course's measures of a page's speed, like **LCP**, how long until the biggest thing on the page appears, and **INP**, how quickly the page reacts to a tap, will show.

**A page that's empty until the JavaScript runs.** By default, a React app's HTML arrives with nothing in it, and JavaScript builds the page in the browser. That's fine for an app behind a login and bad for a page that search engines need to read. The next lesson is about exactly this, and the ways around it.

**Something new to learn.** React has rules of its own, like hooks, keys, and never changing state directly, and when something goes wrong, you debug React's way of doing things on top of the DOM's.

**Upkeep.** React and the libraries around it change often. Upgrades take time, and advice from a few years ago can be out of date.

## When plain HTML or a lighter tool wins

- **A page that's mostly for reading**, like a blog, documentation, a restaurant's menu, or a company's home page. HTML and CSS load faster and work without JavaScript, maybe made by a tool that turns **Markdown**, plain text with simple marks for headings, lists, and links, into pages.
- **A form that sends data and shows the next page.** A plain HTML form does that already, as the web course showed.
- **A little interactivity on a page that's otherwise plain**, like a menu that opens or a photo gallery. A few lines of JavaScript do it. So do small libraries like **htmx**, which swaps in HTML from the server when you click, and **Alpine.js**, which adds small behaviors right in the HTML.
- **A content site with a few interactive spots.** Tools like **Astro** send plain HTML and add JavaScript only where a page needs it, and can use React for just those spots. The next lesson calls these spots islands.

The rule of thumb: React earns its cost when the page is really an app, with a lot of state, shown in many places, changing as people use it. A shop with a cart, filters, reviews, and a checkout is one of those, which is why the course builds one.

The next lesson, Where HTML Is Made, looks at that empty first page, and at the ways to send real HTML instead.

The page itself, `index.html`, is less than half a kilobyte, and the pictures and CSS are a few kilobytes each. The JavaScript file is the big one: 222.44 kB, or 69.28 kB compressed. The starter app is a heading, three pictures, and a button that counts, so nearly all of that is React and React DOM. That's the starting price of every React page, paid before your own code adds anything. The letters in each file name, like `GpEN3EET`, are a fingerprint of the file's contents, which the web course explained lets browsers keep a copy for as long as they like. The Starting a New React Project lesson makes this project and explains every file.

recap:
- Keeping the DOM in step with data by hand means writing every update for every change, and a forgotten one fails quietly.
- Rebuilding everything with innerHTML can't forget an update, but it loses focus, typing, scroll position, and listeners.
- jQuery shortened the steps, Backbone and AngularJS tied views to models, and React let you describe the UI again and changed only the difference.
- In React, the UI is a function of state: components take data and return elements, data flows down as props, and events flow up.
- React compares each new element tree with the last one, which is called diffing, and changes only the DOM that differs.
- react holds components and hooks, react-dom puts them in a browser, and a build step like Vite turns JSX and TypeScript into JavaScript.
- Routing, server data, and the server come from other tools, like React Router, TanStack Query, and Next.js.
- React costs JavaScript to download and run, so it earns its place on app-like pages, not on pages that are mostly for reading.
